questions.title: Why choose an LLM solely for feature engineering instead of end‑to‑end prediction?
questions.question_body: I'm trying to understand why FeatLLM uses an LLM only during preprocessing (to extract rules) instead of letting it predict every sample at inference time. Specifically, what practical advantages does this design have over traditional approaches that perform inference post‑each query?

questions.title: How does the two‑step reasoning instruction prevent learning spurious associations?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that splitting reasoning into (step 1 – infer causal relation without samples + step 2 – derive class‐specific rules using demonstrations) avoids picking up noise‐only correlations among irrelevant columns. Can someone explain intuitively why separating these steps makes the model immune (or less sensitive?) to spurious correlations inferred purely from few demonstrations?

questions.title: What exact textual format does FeatLLM expect when receiving generated rules?
questions.question_body: I see references under *Prompt Design* mentioning “specific response format” expressed during training prompts (Figure 2). Could someone give a concrete example—including headers、“Class = ” label placement and rule syntax—that would satisfy parsing requirements without triggering ECOS’ Naïve‑Program code extractor?   Also note that recipes explicitly forbid “#” symbols in prompts.

questions.title: How does FeatLLM transform noisy natural‑language rules into executable program code?
questions.question_body: After extracting rules via an LLM prompt, *Rule Parsing* calls directly `exec()` on generated Python snippets (Figure 3). Given that the ruled strings can vary subtly (e.g., "greater than" vs ">"), how robust is this dynamic parsing stage against syntax variations or minor typos introduced by the language model?

questions.title: Can you explain how bagging selects samples/feature subsets during ensemble construction?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions bagging randomise both examples AND features when creating regulation trials (“bagging helps reduce prompt size”). What concrete strategy determines which permutations subset in each trial (*e.g.*, sampling proportion of data points or number of buckets)? How many draws are taken per class before averaging probabilities?
